case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
case.limits: Section 512 protects storage at a user's direction. A provider that generates the material itself is not obviously storing anything at anyone's direction.
case.holding: The section 512(c) safe harbour requires knowledge of specific infringing material, not a general awareness that infringement occurs on a service.
case.case_name: Viacom International, Inc. v. YouTube, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The template for platform-layer defenses now raised by model hosts and AI marketplaces: liability attaches to what you were told about specific material, not to what you could have guessed about your users in general.

reading.body:
The Second Circuit's 2012 ruling in *Viacom v. YouTube* established that a platform escapes copyright liability only when it lacked knowledge of specific infringing material, not merely because it had no general awareness that infringement was happening at scale.

That distinction matters directly for AI. Model hosts and AI marketplaces facing training-data copyright claims have begun invoking section 512(c) as a first line of defense. The Viacom holding sets the terms of that argument: liability attaches to what a provider was actually told about identified material, and willful blindness to specific items can defeat the safe harbour, but a diffuse suspicion that users or datasets contain infringing content does not. The data records 79 live cases where this precedent is now in play, including suits against OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and X.AI.

The case also carries a boundary the data makes explicit: section 512(c) covers storage at a user's direction, and a provider that generates material itself is not obviously doing that. Whether AI model training or inference constitutes user-directed storage, rather than generation, is the open question this ruling frames but does not answer. The data does not indicate how any of the 79 live cases has resolved that question.
